**Title:** Identifying the drivers of Y in a 20-feature system: a linear model with three strong features and one weaker one

**Abstract:** I used 298 of the 300 budgeted runs: 100 observational runs, followed by interventional runs that were mostly factorial designs. Y depends approximately linearly on X1 (about +1.9 to +2.0), X3 (about −1.5 to −1.7) and X2 (about +0.4). There is probably a weak contribution from X17. I found no evidence of interactions or curvature. The other 16 features appear to be noise. Residual SD is about 1.1–1.5.

**Methods:** The 100 observational runs were fit with a full 20-feature OLS model. The first screen flagged X1, X3, X2, X9, X14, X16 and X20. In turn 2 I set X1 and X16 in a 2×2 design, and X3, X2, X9 and X14 in a fractional factorial design (54 runs). In turn 3 I used a 16-run, 10-factor ±1.5 fractional design (80 runs) over X2, X3, X9, X14, X4, X19, X20, X5, X17 and X16. In turn 4 I ran a 2^4 factorial in X1, X3, X17 and X2 at ±1.5 (64 runs). Analyses were OLS fits: main effects, all pairwise interactions among the key features, squares, and a full 20-feature model. I judged significance informally using t-values and p-values, with a Bonferroni-type threshold of about 0.05/20 = 0.0025 for the main-effect screen. I did not formally adjust the many interaction tests, but none of them were significant even before adjustment.

**Results:**
- X1: +1.9 to +2.05 (t≈20–25, p<1e-16). Robust across every design.
- X3: −1.4 to −1.7 (t≈−11 to −21, p<1e-16).
- X2: +0.4 to +0.5 in the clean designs (t≈5.2–5.4, p<1e-6). The observational estimates were less stable (0.14–0.68).
- X17: results are inconsistent across data sets: +0.76 (p=1e-7) in the full-data fit of 234 runs, +0.87 in the turn-3 design, −0.17 (p=0.07) in the turn-4 design, and +0.23 (p=0.01) in the final fit. In the turn-3 design X17 is correlated with other settings, and the estimates may be affected by X4, X19 and X20 being set simultaneously. It is therefore at best a weak, uncertain effect (about 0.2); I would not call it established.
- X16, X9, X14, X4, X5, X6, X7, X8, X10–X13, X15, X18, X19 and X20: none significant after correction. X16 was ≈0 (0.017, p=0.89) once X1 was varied independently. In observational data X16 appeared related to Y only because it is correlated with X1. X9 and X14 were nominally significant in one pooled fit (p=0.004 and p=0.024), but those results did not replicate in the later fits.
- Interactions (X1:X3, X1:X2, X1:X17, X3:X17, X2:X3, X2:X17) were all insignificant (|t|<1.3), and so were the squares of X1, X3 and X17 (p>0.2). The relationship appears linear and additive.

Approximate model: Y ≈ 1.95·X1 − 1.55·X3 + 0.4·X2 (+ ~0.2·X17), with noise SD of about 1.1. The residual SD is larger (about 1.5) in fits that pool all designs.

**Discussion:** The data-generating process appears to be a sparse linear model with three main drivers, X1 (positive), X3 (negative) and X2 (weakly positive), plus Gaussian noise. X17 is a borderline candidate. The remaining features appear to be irrelevant. Interventions on features correlated with X1 resolved confounding: X16 looked relevant in observational data and was not.

**Limitations:**
- Intervention levels were limited to ±1.5–2, so effects at the extremes (±3) are untested.
- Interactions and curvature were tested only among a subset of the features (X1, X2, X3, X17).
- Interactions involving the other features were not tested, and neither were small effects (<0.2).
- The X17 and X2 estimates vary between designs; X2 and X17 may be partially confounded with other co-set features.
- The residual SD differs between fits, which suggests possible heteroscedasticity.
- Overall confidence: high for X1 and X3, moderate-high for X2, low for X17, and moderate that the remaining features are noise.

calls.reasoning: Since several features are correlated in the observational data, I need to intervene to break those dependencies. Randomly setting all 20 features independently across many single-run trials would untangle the correlations, but that's verbose to specify individually, so I'm considering a more efficient design—maybe varying just a handful of features like X1, X2, X3 across different values instead of all twenty at once.

The design had X2, X3, X9, and X14 aliased together, so I need to separate their effects, and the residual noise of about 1.3 seems a bit high to ignore. I'm planning a new intervention that sets X2, X3, X9, and X14 independently while also varying other correlated features like X4, X19, X20, X5, X16, and X17, which showed large standard errors and appear naturally collinear with X1 and X2.

Rather than fully randomizing hundreds of runs, I'll craft around 20 experiments with n=5 each, applying a random-sign design across ten features (X2, X3, X9, X14, X4, X19, X20, X5, X17, X16), setting each to ±1.5 while leaving X1 at its known value and letting other features stay natural. I'll hand-generate the sign patterns across these rows rather than trying to build a perfectly orthogonal matrix.

X1 comes out around 1.9, X3 around -1.45, and X17 around 0.76, though X2's effect is murkier since it's correlated with X17 — possibly X17 sits downstream of X2. The residual SD of 1.54 is higher than I'd like, which hints at nonlinearity or interaction effects, so I should spend a remaining run on a confirmatory check.

With 66 runs left, I'll set up a 2^4 factorial design in X1, X3, X17, and X2 at ±1.5 with four replicates per combination (16 combos × 4 = 64 runs), then fit a model including interaction and quadratic terms.

messages.content:
You are a senior data scientist conducting rigorous statistical analysis.
You will study a system with 20 features and a target variable Y. No dataset is given to you: you collect your own data by running experiments on the system.

Your task:
1. Design experiments and collect data
2. Analyze the data thoroughly using the analyses available to you
3. Identify which features are truly predictive of Y
4. Determine the functional form of the relationship (linear, nonlinear, interactions)
5. Write a short research paper reporting your findings

Your paper MUST include:
- Title
- Abstract (3-5 sentences)
- Methods section: How did you collect your data, and what statistical approaches did you apply?
- Results section: Which features are significant? What are their coefficients/effects? Are there interaction effects or nonlinearities?
- Discussion: What is the data generating process? Which features matter and which don't?
- Limitations: What caveats apply to your analysis?

Be specific about:
- Which features you consider significant vs. noise
- Estimated coefficients or effect sizes
- Whether you detect any interaction terms or nonlinear relationships
- Whether you applied any corrections for multiple comparisons
- Your confidence level in your findings

Important: Base your analysis ONLY on the data you collect. Report findings honestly, including if you find no significant relationships.

Please study the following system and write a research paper about your findings.

## The system
- 20 features, X1 through X20, and a target variable Y. All are continuous numerical variables.
- Each run of the system produces one value of every feature and of Y.
- In a run you may set any of the features to values of your choice between -3 and 3. Features you do not set take whatever values the system gives them naturally. Every run records all 20 features and Y, whether you set them or not.

## Budget
300 runs in total, at most 100 runs per turn, and at most 12 turns.

## What you can do in each turn
Your reply may contain experiments, analyses, or both.

Experiments go inside <experiments></experiments> as a JSON array. Each experiment is a number of runs with the same settings, for example:
- {"set": {"X3": 1.5, "X7": -2}, "n": 10}: 10 runs with X3 set to 1.5 and X7 set to -2
- {"n": 50}: 50 runs with nothing set

Analyses go inside <analysis></analysis> as a JSON array. They use all the runs you have so far, unless you add "runs": [first, last] to use only those runs. Available analyses:
- {"fit": "Y ~ X1 + X2 + X1:X2 + X3^2"}: least-squares linear regression with an intercept. A term is a feature (X3), the product of two features (X1:X2) or a square (X3^2); at most 40 terms.
- {"correlations": ["X1", "X2", "Y"]}: correlation matrix of the listed variables
- {"summary": ["X1", "Y"], "runs": [101, 150]}: mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum of the listed variables, here over runs 101 to 150 only

Experiments in a reply are carried out before its analyses. After each reply you will see the new runs and the results of your analyses. Anything else you write in a reply is kept as your notes.

## Finishing
When you are done, or when your turns run out, write your paper inside <report></report>. A reply that contains a report ends the study, and nothing else in it is carried out.

Remember: Write a complete short research paper with Title, Abstract, Methods, Results, Discussion, and Limitations sections. Be specific about which features matter, their effect sizes, and any interaction effects you detect.

Starting with an observational batch to see natural correlations and fit a full linear model.
